system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2152-12-03 00:00:00 to 2152-12-11 13:41:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease status post kidney transplant, calciphylaxis, and peripheral vascular disease was admitted for altered mental status one day after discharge. He was found to have toxic metabolic encephalopathy likely due to opioid toxicity, as his confusion resolved after reducing his OxyContin and oxycodone doses. Workup showed no infection or acute intracranial process. His chronic left leg wound from recent necrotizing fasciitis debridement remained stable without infection, and dry gangrene in the fingers was non-progressive. Hypertension was managed with multiple agents, including increasing the clonidine patch. Kidney function improved slightly, with discharge creatinine of 2.5, and transplant medications were continued without rejection. He was discharged home with adjusted pain medications, wound care instructions, and close outpatient follow-up.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you at ___ 
___.  During your hospitalization, you had surgery to 
remove unhealthy tissue on your lower extremity.  You tolerated 
the procedure well and are now ready to be discharged from the 
hospital.   Please follow the recommendations below to ensure a 
speedy and uneventful recovery.

LOWER  EXTREMITY AMPUTATION 
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS
ACTIVITY 
You should keep your amputation site elevated and straight 
whenever possible.  This will prevent swelling of the stump and 
maintain flexibility in your joint.  
It is very important that you put no weight or pressure on your 
stump with activity or at rest to allow the wound to heal 
properly. 
You may use the opposite foot for transfers and pivots, if 
applicable.  It will take time to learn to use a walker and 
learn to transfer into and out of a wheelchair.  

MEDICATION
Before you leave the hospital, you will be given a list of all 
the medicine you should take at home.  If a medication that you 
normally take is not on the list or a medication that you do not 
take is on the list please discuss it with the team!  
You will likely be prescribed narcotic pain medication on 
discharge which  can be very constipating.  If you take 
narcotics,  please also take a stool softener such as Colace.   
If constipation becomes a problem, your pharmacist can suggest 
an additional over the counter laxative. 
You should take Tylenol ___ every 6 hours, as needed for 
pain.  If this is not enough, take your prescription narcotic 
pain medication.  You should require less pain medication each 
day.  Do not take more than a daily total of 3000mg of Tylenol.  
Tylenol is used as an ingredient in some other over-the-counter 
and prescription medications.  Be aware of how much Tylenol you 
are taking in a day.

BATHING/SHOWERING: 
You may shower when you feel strong enough but no tub baths or 
pools until you have permission from your surgeon and the 
incision is fully healed.
After your shower, gently dry the incision well.   Do not rub 
the area. 

WOUND CARE:
Please keep the wound clean and dry. It is very important that 
there is no pressure on the stump. If there is no drainage, you 
may leave the incision open to air.  
Your staples/sutures will remain in for at least 4 weeks.  At 
your followup appointment, we will see if the incision has 
healed enough to remove the staples. 
Before you can be fitted for prosthesis (a man-made limb to 
replace the limb that was removed) your incision needs to be 
fully healed. 

CALL THE OFFICE FOR: ___
Opening, bleeding or drainage or odor from your stump incision 
Redness, swelling or warmth in your stump.
Fever greater than 101 degrees, chills, or worsening 
incisional/stump pain  

NO OTHER PROVIDER, EXCEPT YOUR VASCULAR SURGEON, SHOULD 
DETERMINE IF YOUR STAPLES ARE READY TO BE REMOVED FROM YOUR 
STUMP!   
IF THERE ARE ANY QUESTIONS, THE PROVIDER SHOULD CALL THE 
VASCULAR SURGERY OFFICE AT ___ TO DISCUSS. THE STAPLES 
WILL BE REMOVED IN THE OFFICE AT YOUR FOLLOWUP APPOINTMENT WHEN 
IT IS DETERMINED BY THE VASCULAR SURGEON THAT THE WOUND HAS 
SUFFICIENTLY HEALED.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you at ___ 
___.  During your hospitalization, you had surgery to 
remove unhealthy tissue on your lower extremity.  You tolerated 
the procedure well and are now ready to be discharged from the 
hospital.   Please follow the recommendations below to ensure a 
speedy and uneventful recovery.

LOWER  EXTREMITY AMPUTATION 
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS
ACTIVITY 
You should keep your amputation site elevated and straight 
whenever possible.  This will prevent swelling of the stump and 
maintain flexibility in your joint.  
It is very important that you put no weight or pressure on your 
stump with activity or at rest to allow the wound to heal 
properly. 
You may use the opposite foot for transfers and pivots, if 
applicable.  It will take time to learn to use a walker and 
learn to transfer into and out of a wheelchair.  

MEDICATION
Before you leave the hospital, you will be given a list of all 
the medicine you should take at home.  If a medication that you 
normally take is not on the list or a medication that you do not 
take is on the list please discuss it with the team!  
You will likely be prescribed narcotic pain medication on 
discharge which  can be very constipating.  If you take 
narcotics,  please also take a stool softener such as Colace.   
If constipation becomes a problem, your pharmacist can suggest 
an additional over the counter laxative. 
You should take Tylenol ___ every 6 hours, as needed for 
pain.  If this is not enough, take your prescription narcotic 
pain medication.  You should require less pain medication each 
day.  Do not take more than a daily total of 3000mg of Tylenol.  
Tylenol is used as an ingredient in some other over-the-counter 
and prescription medications.  Be aware of how much Tylenol you 
are taking in a day.

BATHING/SHOWERING: 
You may shower when you feel strong enough but no tub baths or 
pools until you have permission from your surgeon and the 
incision is fully healed.
After your shower, gently dry the incision well.   Do not rub 
the area. 

WOUND CARE:
Please keep the wound clean and dry. It is very important that 
there is no pressure on the stump. If there is no drainage, you 
may leave the incision open to air.  
Your staples/sutures will remain in for at least 4 weeks.  At 
your followup appointment, we will see if the incision has 
healed enough to remove the staples. 
Before you can be fitted for prosthesis (a man-made limb to 
replace the limb that was removed) your incision needs to be 
fully healed. 

CALL THE OFFICE FOR: ___
Opening, bleeding or drainage or odor from your stump incision 
Redness, swelling or warmth in your stump.
Fever greater than 101 degrees, chills, or worsening 
incisional/stump pain

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , part of your surgical team. I understand you've been having a lot of pain in your left leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It’s been terrible—sharp, constant pain. I can’t even touch it without wincing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve reviewed your history. You have severe peripheral vascular disease and diabetes, and the left leg has been affected by calciphylaxis and infection. The Achilles tendon is exposed and necrotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what does that mean? Is it worse now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, yes. The tissue is dying and infected. We believe the best option is to remove the affected part of your leg to stop the infection from spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Amputation? You mean… cutting off my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re planning a below-knee amputation. It’s a two-step process. Tomorrow, we’ll do a guillotine amputation—removing the leg quickly to control the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once the infection is under control and swelling goes down, we’ll do a second surgery to reshape and close the stump properly. That’s called a re-amputation with closure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many surgeries… I’m scared it won’t heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your kidney transplant and diabetes do make healing harder. But leaving this infection untreated is much more dangerous. We’ll give you strong IV antibiotics starting today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… what antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole. They cover the most likely bacteria. Infectious disease helped us choose them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need blood transfusions again? Last time I felt so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low at 7.5, so we may need to give you blood before surgery. It helps your body handle the stress and improves healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my other medicines—my transplant drugs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll keep taking tacrolimus. The nephrology team is helping us manage your levels. We’ll check a level tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to lose the kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. Your blood pressure has been fluctuating, so we’re adjusting your nifedipine and labetalol to protect your kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain? The OxyContin isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted pain management. After surgery, you’ll get Dilaudid through a PCA pump—press a button when you need it. We’ll also start Lyrica to help with nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake during the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’ll be under general anesthesia. We’ll also do a spinal block to help with pain afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished your pre-op chest X-ray. Lungs look clear, heart size normal. You’re good to go for surgery tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about my lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___ , you’re back from surgery. The guillotine amputation went well. We removed the infected part of your leg below the knee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How’s the wound? Is it… open?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we left it open for now to allow drainage and monitor for infection. We’ll close it in about three days once we’re sure things are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got two units before surgery. Your hematocrit went from 20 to 25.1. That’s a good improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain team adjusted your meds. You’re on Dilaudid PCA, Lyrica, and your usual OxyContin. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The PCA helps a lot. But I’m a bit dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. We added baclofen yesterday for muscle spasms, but if it’s making you too sleepy, we can stop it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I can’t think straight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discontinue it. Your tacrolimus level was 4.3 this morning—on the low side—so we increased the dose to 4 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re monitoring closely. Your creatinine is stable at 1.4. That’s good for someone with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound looks clean—no signs of infection. We’re planning the second surgery—closure—tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re healing well. We’ll give you one unit of blood before surgery to boost your hemoglobin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery went well. We closed the stump and put in staples. The dressing is on now—we’ll remove it in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does it hurt more now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might feel tighter, but we’ve adjusted your pain meds. You’re now on oral Dilaudid as needed, plus acetaminophen and Lyrica.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We took the dressing off. The wound looks excellent—clean, dry, no redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start moving around?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with help. You can sit in a wheelchair, but don’t put any weight on the stump. Physical therapy will help you learn to transfer safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my hand? The fingers are still black.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hand surgery saw you. The dry gangrene in your second and fourth fingers isn’t infected. No urgent surgery needed. You can follow up as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vancomycin trough was 18.6—good level. We’ll switch cipro and metronidazole to pills. Vancomycin will continue through your port for four more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll still get IV meds at the rehab center?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a nurse will give it daily. We’re also sending you with a clonidine patch for blood pressure and increasing your nifedipine to 90 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue glargine at bedtime and use sliding scale regular insulin as needed. Keep checking your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow to an extended care facility for rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get a prosthesis someday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Eventually, yes—but only after the wound fully heals, which takes at least four weeks. Staples stay in until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain? Will it ever go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should improve. We’re tapering the narcotics. Keep using Lyrica and acetaminophen. Let the rehab team know if pain flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to leave. Here’s your discharge plan—meds, wound care, and follow-up with vascular surgery in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’m nervous but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right path. Keep the stump elevated, clean, and dry. Call us if you see redness, drainage, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no one else removes the staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Only your vascular surgeon decides when they come out. We’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. You’ve made great progress.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease status post kidney transplant, and severe peripheral vascular disease was admitted for severe left leg pain due to necrotic infection and gangrene. He underwent a two-stage left below-knee amputation: first a guillotine amputation followed by re-amputation with closure. He received blood transfusions preoperatively to support hemoglobin levels and was treated with intravenous vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole for infection, later transitioning to oral antibiotics. Pain was managed with a Dilaudid PCA initially, then oral hydromorphone, acetaminophen, and pregabalin. The nephrology team optimized tacrolimus and blood pressure medications to protect his transplant. The wound healed well, and he was discharged to extended care with plans for rehabilitation and outpatient follow-up. His right hand showed dry gangrene of multiple digits, but no acute intervention was needed.
